title: National Airlines 2511
summary: National Airlines Flight 2511, a Douglas DC-6 operating from New York to Miami, exploded in mid-air near Bolivia, North Carolina on January 6, 1960. The aircraft broke up in flight, with wreckage scattered over a wide area including pieces found 25 miles from the main crash site. Civil Aeronautics Board investigation concluded that the probable cause was a dynamite explosion located beneath the right-side seat of row 7. The explosion was determined to be a suicide bombing committed by a passenger seeking to commit insurance fraud, though the bomber's widow ultimately could not collect on policies when the death was ruled a suicide.
probable_cause: Malicious destruction of aircraft through dynamite explosion in the passenger cabin, placed beneath seat row 7 and detonated by passenger seeking to commit insurance fraud. Structural damage from the explosion forced the aircraft into an uncontrollable descent that resulted in in-flight disintegration.

factors.evidence: Dynamite explosion in passenger cabin beneath seat row 7
Explosion severely damaged structural integrity of fuselage
Aircraft descended uncontrollably after structural damage
Aircraft debris caught fire on impact

title: Avianca 671
summary: Avianca Flight 671, a Lockheed L-1049E Super Constellation, crashed on landing at Montego Bay Airport, Jamaica on January 21, 1960. The aircraft experienced a heavy touchdown followed by a bounce and landing back on the runway. The aircraft then skidded down the runway in flames, coming to rest upside down approximately 1,900 feet from the runway threshold. Investigation found no evidence of technical defects or improper maintenance. The aircraft's sinking speed on approach was greater than the safe design limit, requiring a rapid descent of more than 1,200 feet per minute from one nautical mile out. The hard landing with excessive vertical velocity exceeded aircraft design limits, causing structural damage that led to fuel spillage and fire.
probable_cause: Hard landing with excessive sinking speed and vertical velocity beyond aircraft design limits, likely resulting from approach instability and excessive descent rate on final approach. Contributing factors included possible crew fatigue and training deficiencies in landing technique assessment.

factors.evidence: Aircraft was undesirably high on approach one nautical mile from threshold
Aircraft touched down with sinking speed exceeding design limits
Impact damage from hard landing caused structural failure
Left wing broke off, fuel spillage led to intense post-landing fire

events.text: Flight originated at Miami International Airport with 46 passengers and 7 crew
Aircraft on landing approach at Montego Bay in overcast with intermittent rain
Heavy touchdown, aircraft bounced then landed back on runway, skidded in flames
Aircraft came to rest upside down 1,900 feet from threshold, 37 of 46 killed

title: Northwest Orient Airlines 710
summary: Northwest Airlines Flight 710 was a scheduled flight between Minneapolis, Minnesota and Miami, Florida, with a stop in Chicago. On March 17, 1960, the six-month-old Lockheed L-188 Electra operating the flight broke up in midair in southern Indiana, near Cannelton, killing all 63 people on board. title: 1960 New York air disaster
summary: Two aircraft collided in mid-air, destroying both aircraft. Operating United Airlines, a Douglas DC-8, crashed killing all 134 people aboard. Navigation errors and loss of situational awareness were found to contribute significantly. The accident set records for aviation safety as one of the deadliest incidents of its time.
